title: When the lesion is everywhere: coma and diffuse disease
description: How to localize a child who cannot cooperate: the two places consciousness lives, the coma exam as a level-finder, metabolic versus structural coma, herniation, and diffuse disease.
why: Some findings point to no single level, and that is itself a localization.
objectives: Explain why depressed consciousness localizes to the brainstem tegmentum or to both hemispheres, and what a one-sided lesion must do to cause coma.
Use breathing, pupils, eye movements and motor responses to place a coma at one level, or to recognize that the signs do not agree.
Separate metabolic and toxic coma from structural coma at the bedside, and act on the difference.
Recognize uncal herniation from the pupil, and explain why the hemiparesis may sit on the wrong side.
Treat diffuse and multifocal disease in a child as an address in its own right, and carry it into a differential.

sections.title: Consciousness lives in two places
sections.content:
Every other module in this curriculum asks the patient to do something: squeeze, follow, walk, report a pinprick. A child in coma can do none of it, and that is exactly why this module belongs in a course on localization. When the patient cannot cooperate, the anatomy has to speak through reflexes, and the first reflex worth reading is consciousness itself.

**Two structures, working together**

Wakefulness depends on an interaction between the **ascending reticular activating system** in the brainstem and the **cerebral hemispheres** (Brazis 2011, p. 604). In people, the activating system lies in the paramedian tegmentum of the pons and midbrain. That gives coma only two honest addresses: a lesion in that small tegmental core, or dysfunction of **both** hemispheres at once.

The consequence is a rule with real bedside force. A lesion confined to **one hemisphere** does not, on its own, abolish consciousness. A child with a large one-sided stroke or tumour may be aphasic, hemiplegic and miserable, but awake. If that child becomes unresponsive, something has changed: the lesion has grown or swollen enough to press on the brainstem, a second process has appeared on the other side, or the child is seizing without convulsing. Unresponsiveness in a child with a one-sided lesion is therefore a **new localizing sign**, and usually an emergency.

**Say what you saw**

Words such as lethargic, obtunded and stuporous feel precise and are not. Brazis argues for describing responsiveness in plain words: what the child did, to which stimulus, and how quickly it faded (Brazis 2011, p. 603). "Opened her eyes to her name, looked at her mother, then drifted off without speaking" can be compared at the next examination by someone else; "lethargic" cannot. In a child the stimuli are different, a parent's voice, a favourite toy, a feed, but the principle holds: record the behaviour, not the label.

The rest of this module applies the same discipline to the brainstem reflexes, which keep working when the child cannot, and to the diffuse diseases that make "everywhere" an answer rather than a failure to localize.
keyPoints: Consciousness needs the brainstem reticular activating system (paramedian tegmentum of the pons and midbrain) and both hemispheres (Brazis 2011, p. 604).
A lesion confined to one hemisphere does not cause coma on its own; coma in that setting means brainstem compression, a second lesion or non-convulsive seizures.
Describe responsiveness in plain words, naming the stimulus and the response, rather than with labels such as lethargic or stuporous (Brazis 2011, p. 603).
When the child cannot cooperate, the reflexes of the brainstem become the examination.

question.question: A 9-year-old with a known left frontal tumour has been awake and talking with a right hemiparesis. Overnight she becomes hard to rouse: she opens her eyes only to a firm sternal rub and does not speak. What does the change in consciousness tell you?
options: Nothing new about localization: the tumour is in the left hemisphere and hemispheric lesions cause sleepiness
A new process is involving the brainstem or the other hemisphere, such as swelling with herniation or non-convulsive seizures, and it needs urgent assessment
The tumour has spread along the corticospinal tract, which explains both the weakness and the drowsiness
She is post-ictal after an unwitnessed seizure, so observation without imaging is appropriate
question.explanation: Consciousness depends on the brainstem reticular activating system and both hemispheres together, so a lesion confined to one hemisphere does not abolish it. A child with a one-sided tumour who becomes unresponsive has a new problem: swelling compressing the brainstem, a second lesion, or seizures without convulsions. Treating it as an expected feature of a hemispheric tumour misses that it is a new localizing sign. Spread along the corticospinal tract would worsen weakness, not explain coma. A post-ictal state is possible, but it is a conclusion you reach after excluding herniation and ongoing seizures, not a reason to skip imaging and an EEG.

sections.title: The coma exam as a level-finder
sections.content:
The coma examination is localization with the patient's cooperation removed. Four things still work without effort from the child, and each has a level written into it: the **pattern of breathing**, the **pupils**, the **eye movements** and the **motor response to pain** (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-97). Use the figure above to set each one and watch whether they agree.

**Breathing.** Waxing and waning breathing with pauses (Cheyne-Stokes) points to both hemispheres or the diencephalon. Sustained, fast, deep breathing points to the low midbrain or upper pons; long pauses at full inspiration (apneustic breathing) to the pons; chaotic, irregular breathing to the medulla, where the respiratory rhythm is generated (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-95).

**Pupils.** Small pupils that still react fit diencephalic or metabolic depression (Brazis 2011, p. 608). A midbrain lesion interrupts the light reflex, and the pupils lose their reactivity. A pontine lesion cuts the descending sympathetic fibres and leaves pinpoint pupils (Pearl 2014, p. 95).

**Eye movements.** With the head turned, the eyes of a comatose child with an intact brainstem float to the opposite side, like an expensive doll's eyes (Pearl 2014, p. 96). Cold water in the ear is a stronger stimulus: the eyes should turn toward the ice. If they do, the brainstem from upper medulla to midbrain is working. There is no fast phase in coma, because nystagmus needs the cortex.

**Motor response.** Flexion of the arms with extended legs places the lesion between cortex and upper midbrain; extension of all four limbs places it from midbrain to the pontomedullary junction; flaccidity, below that (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

**Putting it together.** If breathing, pupils, eyes and posture all point to the same level, a single structural lesion there fits. If they **disagree**, the process is probably multifocal, and multifocal coma is most often metabolic. If they **move downward** over hours, think herniation (Pearl 2014, p. 97). Children are scored with modified versions of the adult coma scales (Pearl 2014, p. 147), but the level-finding logic is the same at every age.
keyPoints: Breathing, pupils, eye movements and motor responses each point to a level, and they keep working when the child cannot cooperate (Pearl 2014, pp. 94-97).
Pinpoint pupils with apneustic breathing and absent horizontal eye movements point to the pons; small reactive pupils fit diencephalic or metabolic depression (Brazis 2011, p. 608).
Eyes that turn toward cold water in the ear show the brainstem from medulla to midbrain is working.
Signs that agree suggest one structural lesion; signs that disagree suggest multifocal, usually metabolic, disease; signs that move downward suggest herniation (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

question.question: A 12-year-old is found unresponsive. She has long pauses at the top of each breath, pinpoint pupils, no horizontal eye movement when the head is turned, and extends all four limbs to pain. Where is the lesion, and what kind of process does the pattern suggest?
options: Both hemispheres, from a metabolic cause, because she is in coma
The medulla, because breathing is abnormal
The pons, from a single structural lesion, because every sign points to the same level
The midbrain, because extensor posturing always means a midbrain lesion
question.explanation: Apneustic breathing, pinpoint pupils, absent horizontal doll's-eye movements and extensor posturing all point to the pons. When every sign agrees on one level, a single structural lesion there is the best fit, which in a child means looking urgently for haemorrhage, a vascular event or a pontine tumour. Hemispheric or metabolic coma gives small reactive pupils and intact doll's eyes, not pinpoint pupils with lost horizontal movement. Medullary breathing is chaotic rather than apneustic. Extensor posturing marks the span from midbrain to the pontomedullary junction, so it agrees with a pontine lesion rather than pinning the midbrain on its own.

sections.title: Metabolic or structural?
sections.content:
The most useful decision at the bedside of a comatose child is not which level but **which kind**: is a structural lesion pressing on the brain, or is the brain being poisoned or starved? The two are managed differently, and one of them can often be corrected within minutes.

**The clue that the books keep returning to**

In metabolic coma the **pupils may still react when the eye movements are gone** (Brazis 2011, p. 610). The pupillary light reflex is one of the most resistant reflexes in the brainstem. A structural lesion that destroys horizontal eye movements usually takes the pupils with it, because the pathways sit close together. A drug or a metabolic derangement can silence the eye movements while the small pupils still constrict to light. That dissociation, reactive pupils with absent eye movements, points away from a structural brainstem lesion and toward the blood.

**Drugs can do anything**

Pearl's caveat is worth memorizing: drugs can do anything (Pearl 2014, p. 96). Anticholinergics and stimulants dilate the pupils; barbiturates, benzodiazepines and other sedatives constrict them. Most sedative overdoses do not abolish the light reflex (Brazis 2011, p. 608). A toddler who has found a grandparent's tablets can produce a coma examination that mimics almost any level.

**What points to structure**

Asymmetry is the friend of the structural diagnosis: one pupil larger than the other, a gaze deviation, a hemiparesis, posturing on one side. So is a pattern that **descends** over hours. Symmetry, fluctuation and signs that refuse to agree on a level point the other way (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

**In a child**

The metabolic list in children is long and urgent: low glucose, ingestion, high ammonia, diabetic ketoacidosis, infection, and non-convulsive seizures, which are a reason to involve the [EEG curriculum](/eeg) early. The rule is simple even when the list is not: check the glucose at once, look for a chemical cause while you examine, and image urgently whenever the examination is asymmetric or worsening.
keyPoints: Reactive pupils with absent eye movements is the classic sign of metabolic or toxic coma (Brazis 2011, p. 610).
Drugs can do anything to the pupils: anticholinergics and stimulants dilate, sedatives constrict (Pearl 2014, p. 96).
Asymmetry and a descending pattern point to a structural lesion; symmetry and signs that disagree point to metabolic disease.
In every comatose child, check the glucose immediately and look for a chemical cause while the examination proceeds.

question.question: A 2-year-old is brought in very drowsy after playing unsupervised at a relative's house. Her pupils are small and react briskly to light, she has no horizontal eye movement on head turning, and her limbs are symmetrically floppy. What is the most appropriate interpretation and first step?
options: A pontine haemorrhage, because horizontal eye movements are absent; arrange neurosurgical review before anything else
Probably toxic or metabolic, because the pupils react despite absent eye movements; check the glucose at once and start a toxic and metabolic search, imaging if anything becomes asymmetric
Brain death must be considered, because the doll's-eye response is absent
A functional unresponsiveness, because the examination is symmetric
question.explanation: Reactive pupils in the face of absent eye movements is the dissociation that points to metabolic or toxic coma, and in a toddler with an unsupervised opportunity an ingestion heads the list. The first steps are the ones that can be corrected quickly: glucose, then a toxic and metabolic screen, with imaging if the examination becomes asymmetric or worsens. A pontine haemorrhage usually takes the pupils with the eye movements and leaves pinpoint, poorly reactive pupils. Brain death requires absent brainstem reflexes, including the pupils, which here are working. A symmetric examination is typical of metabolic coma and is no evidence of a functional disorder.

sections.title: Herniation: when the lesion moves
sections.content:
A mass inside a closed skull does not stay where it started. It pushes brain from one compartment into another, and the signs then belong to the place being squeezed rather than the place where the trouble began. Herniation is localization in motion.

**Uncal herniation: trust the pupil**

An expanding mass in one temporal lobe can push the uncus over the edge of the tentorium and onto the third nerve and the midbrain (Pearl 2014, pp. 37, 93). The pupil-constricting fibres run on the outside of the third nerve, so external pressure dilates the pupil early, on the **same side** as the mass. A progressive third-nerve palsy and falling consciousness follow.

The hemiparesis is less reliable. The mass should weaken the opposite side through the corticospinal tract on its own side. But the shifting midbrain can be pressed against the opposite edge of the tentorium, notching the other cerebral peduncle (Kernohan's notch) and weakening the limbs on the **same side** as the mass. Pearl puts the lesson bluntly: in uncal herniation the dilated pupil reliably tells the side of the lesion, and the hemiparesis may not (Pearl 2014, p. 37).

**The other directions**

The cingulate gyrus can slide under the falx and compress the anterior cerebral artery territory, weakening the opposite leg. Swelling of both hemispheres pushes the diencephalon straight down, producing progressive dysfunction of both sides of the brainstem from the top. Cerebellar tonsils pushed through the foramen magnum compress the medulla, and breathing and circulation can fail abruptly (Pearl 2014, pp. 92-93). A widening pulse pressure with a slowing pulse and changing breathing is the body's late warning of raised pressure (Pearl 2014, p. 94).

**Watching the level fall**

The coma signs from section 2 are the best monitor. Breathing that changes from Cheyne-Stokes to sustained hyperventilation, pupils that move from small and reactive to fixed, posturing that moves from flexion to extension: a level that descends over hours is herniation until proved otherwise (Pearl 2014, p. 97). To see it, return to the coma figure in section 2 and press **Watch a herniation descend**: breathing, pupils, eyes and posture change stage by stage, and the level stops being a place and becomes a trajectory. Children's posterior fossa tumours make the downward, tonsillar direction a particular concern, and a lumbar puncture in a child with signs of raised pressure and a mass can precipitate it.
keyPoints: In uncal herniation the pupil on the side of the mass dilates first, because pupillary fibres run on the outside of the third nerve (Pearl 2014, pp. 36-37).
The hemiparesis can be on the same side as the mass (Kernohan's notch), so the pupil, not the weakness, tells the side (Pearl 2014, p. 37).
Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and can stop breathing and circulation abruptly (Pearl 2014, p. 93).
A level that descends over hours on serial coma examinations means herniation until proved otherwise (Pearl 2014, p. 97).

question.question: A 14-year-old is brought in after a fall from a bicycle. He was talking, then became drowsy. His right pupil is dilated and sluggish, and his RIGHT arm and leg are weaker than the left. On which side is the expanding lesion most likely to be?
options: Left, because the hemiparesis is on the right and the corticospinal tract crosses
It cannot be told, because the signs conflict
Both sides equally, so bilateral surgery should be planned
Right, because the dilated pupil reliably marks the side of uncal herniation, and the same-side weakness can come from the opposite peduncle being notched on the tentorium
question.explanation: In uncal herniation the pupil-constricting fibres on the outside of the third nerve are compressed first, so the dilated pupil is on the side of the mass. The weakness can be on the same side when the shifted midbrain presses the opposite cerebral peduncle against the tentorium, Kernohan's notch, which is why the pupil is the more reliable sign. Reading the right hemiparesis in the usual crossed way would point to the wrong side. The signs only seem to conflict if you trust the weakness over the pupil, and nothing here suggests two lesions.

sections.title: False localizing signs
sections.content:
Most of this module has been about signs that agree. These are signs that mislead, or more fairly, answer a question you did not ask. A **false localizing sign** is made by a process at a distance, by pressure, shift or a chemical, rather than by damage at the address the sign usually names.

**The messenger and the address**

[[m07-brainstem|Module 7]] met the child with morning headaches, vomiting and double vision on looking to one side. The sixth nerve's long course makes it an early casualty of raised intracranial pressure from tumours above or below the tentorium, hydrocephalus or pseudotumor cerebri (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 48; Brazis 2011, p. 202). Brazis names sixth-nerve palsy and papilloedema as the commonest false localizing signs, and warns that a supratentorial process, especially a midline one causing hydrocephalus, can raise the pressure without focal signs and leave cranial nerve palsies that look like a posterior fossa lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 622). Posterior fossa tumours are common in children (Pearl 2014, p. 63), so the posterior fossa is a fair suspect, but the sixth nerve only told you that the pressure is up.

**The rest of the family**

- **The wrong-sided hemiparesis** of Kernohan's notch, already met in the herniation section (Brazis 2011, p. 616).
- **A sensory level too low**: compression high in the cervical cord can give a sensory level on the trunk and clumsy, wasted hands (Brazis 2011, p. 115).
- **Nystagmus from drugs**: anticonvulsants can produce a central-looking nystagmus with no lesion in the brainstem (Pearl 2014, p. 121).
- **Anomia**: word-finding failure is relatively nonlocalizing (Pearl 2014, p. 20; [[m09-hemispheres|Module 9]]).

**A sign that does localize**

Contrast vertical gaze. A tumour pressing on the posterior commissure, a pineal tumour for example, disturbs vertical gaze and can hold the eyes tonically downward: Parinaud syndrome (Pearl 2014, p. 40). In a child with raised pressure, failure of upgaze is an address; a sixth-nerve palsy is a messenger.

> **Bedside trick.** When the eyes rest deviated to one side, turn the head passively. The doll's-eye movement overcomes the gaze preference of a cortical lesion, because the brainstem gaze centre still works, but not the gaze palsy of a pontine lesion, where that centre is gone (Pearl 2014, p. 45). The eyes look toward a cortical lesion and away from a pontine one (Pearl 2014, p. 43), so one manoeuvre settles level and side together.

**The rule**

A sign that travels alone deserves suspicion. Ask what company it would keep at a true address; if the company is missing, read the sign as a report on pressure, shift or chemistry, and image the whole head rather than the spot it seems to name.
keyPoints: A false localizing sign is produced at a distance, by pressure, shift or a chemical, not by damage at the address it usually names.
Sixth-nerve palsy and papilloedema are the commonest false localizing signs; a supratentorial or midline process can imitate a posterior fossa lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 622).
Kernohan's notch, a sensory level from high cervical compression, drug-induced nystagmus and anomia all point to the wrong place or nowhere (Brazis 2011, pp. 115, 616; Pearl 2014, pp. 20, 121).
Failure of vertical gaze from pressure on the posterior commissure does localize, to the pineal region (Pearl 2014, p. 40).
Passive head turning overcomes a cortical gaze preference but not a pontine gaze palsy (Pearl 2014, p. 45).

question.question: An 8-year-old has had three weeks of morning headaches and vomiting. Both optic discs are swollen and neither eye abducts fully. There is no facial weakness, no gaze palsy, no ataxia and no long-tract sign. A colleague requests an MRI limited to the pons and posterior fossa. What do you advise?
options: Agree, because posterior fossa tumours are common in children and the sixth nerves arise from the pons
Do a lumbar puncture first to measure the opening pressure, then decide on imaging
Image the orbits to look for disease of the lateral rectus muscles
Image the whole brain urgently, because bilateral sixth-nerve palsies with papilloedema report raised pressure, which a supratentorial or midline process can cause as readily as a posterior fossa one
question.explanation: Sixth-nerve palsy and papilloedema are the commonest false localizing signs: the long sixth nerve suffers from raised pressure wherever its source, and a supratentorial or midline lesion causing hydrocephalus can imitate a posterior fossa one (Brazis 2011, p. 622; Pearl 2014, p. 43). The posterior fossa is a fair suspect in a child (Pearl 2014, p. 63), which is what makes the limited scan tempting, but the palsies do not place the lesion there, and a limited study could miss the cause. A lumbar puncture before imaging in a child with raised pressure risks herniation. Swollen discs point inside the skull, not to the orbit.

sections.title: Diffuse and multifocal disease in children
sections.content:
Localization teaches us to look for the single point where the findings meet. Sometimes there is no such point, and the honest answer is "everywhere". That is not a failure of the method. It is a result, and it narrows the differential as sharply as any address on the [[m01-where-before-what|level ladder]].

**Discrete lesions and system disease**

Brazis draws the distinction clearly: much of localization was learned from discrete lesions such as infarcts, tumours, abscesses and plaques, while other diseases attack whole arrays of neurons that share a job (Brazis 2011, p. 4). The first kind gives signs that meet at one point. The second gives signs that respect a system, a tract or a cell type, rather than a place.

**Three ways a child's brain is everywhere**

- **Diffuse:** an encephalopathy from a toxin, an infection, a metabolic derangement or prolonged seizures. Consciousness falls, the signs are symmetric, and the coma examination refuses to settle on a level.
- **Multifocal:** several discrete lesions at once. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis after an infection is the classic pediatric example: a sleepy child with signs from the hemispheres, the brainstem and the cord that no single lesion can explain.
- **System:** a genetic or metabolic disease that takes one kind of tissue throughout the nervous system, white matter in a leukodystrophy, grey matter in a neuronal storage disease.

**Regression: localization in time**

In a child, "everywhere" often shows itself not as a coma but as a loss: skills that were present and are now gone. Regression localizes the process in time as clearly as a sensory level localizes it in space. It says the disease is active now, and it moves the differential toward the neurodegenerative, genetic and metabolic causes, the epileptic encephalopathies and acquired encephalitis that the next module sets out in its grid.

The decision that follows is the same whatever the pattern: name it (diffuse, multifocal or system), then let tempo choose among the causes. [[m11-where-to-what|Module 11]] builds that grid.
keyPoints: "Everywhere" is a localization: diffuse, multifocal and system patterns each narrow the differential.
Discrete lesions give signs that meet at a point; system diseases give signs that respect a tract or cell type throughout the nervous system (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
Signs from several levels at once in a sleepy child after an infection suggest a multifocal process such as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
Regression, the loss of skills already acquired, localizes a process in time and points toward neurodegenerative, genetic and metabolic causes and epileptic encephalopathy.

question.question: A 6-year-old became sleepy and irritable ten days after a viral illness. She now has a mild left hemiparesis, unsteady arms, double vision and difficulty passing urine. No single lesion explains all of this. What is the most useful way to frame her localization?
options: Multifocal central nervous system disease, which points toward an acute inflammatory demyelinating process and calls for imaging of the brain and the whole spine
Brainstem, because double vision is present, so imaging of the posterior fossa alone is enough
Non-localizing, so localization adds nothing and broad testing should replace it
Peripheral nerve, because the bladder is involved
question.explanation: Signs from a hemisphere (hemiparesis), the brainstem or cerebellar connections (double vision, unsteadiness) and the cord (bladder) cannot come from one lesion. That makes the localization multifocal, which after an infection points toward acute disseminated encephalomyelitis and tells you to image the brain and the whole spine. Choosing the brainstem alone ignores the bladder and the hemiparesis, and imaging only the posterior fossa could miss the cord. "Non-localizing" throws away the information: multifocal is itself a narrowing answer. The peripheral nerve cannot explain drowsiness or double vision with a hemiparesis.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old is comatose after a cardiac arrest. Breathing is Cheyne-Stokes, the pupils are small and reactive, the eyes move fully with head turning, and the arms flex to pain. A colleague asks where the lesion is. What is the best answer?
options: The medulla, because breathing is irregular
Both hemispheres or the diencephalon, with the brainstem working, because every sign points to that level
The pons, because the pupils are small
The midbrain, because there is posturing
quiz.explanation: Cheyne-Stokes breathing, small reactive pupils, intact doll's-eye movements and flexor posturing all point to the level above the midbrain: both hemispheres or the diencephalon, with a working brainstem. That fits a diffuse hypoxic insult. Medullary breathing is chaotic rather than waxing and waning. Pontine pupils are pinpoint, and pontine lesions abolish horizontal doll's-eye movements, which are present here. Flexor posturing places the lesion between cortex and upper midbrain, so it agrees with the hemispheric level rather than pinning the midbrain.

quiz.question: An adolescent is comatose. His pupils react to light, but cold water in either ear produces no eye movement at all, and his limbs are symmetrically flaccid. Breathing is shallow but regular. What does this combination suggest?
options: A structural lesion of the whole brainstem, so the outlook is hopeless
Brain death, because there is no caloric response
A toxic or metabolic cause such as a sedative overdose, because the pupils still react when the eye movements are gone
Locked-in syndrome, because he is not moving
quiz.explanation: The pupillary light reflex is among the most resistant brainstem reflexes, and in metabolic coma the pupils may still react when eye movements cannot be elicited. Reactive pupils with absent calorics therefore point toward a drug or metabolic cause, which may be fully reversible. A structural lesion destroying the brainstem would usually take the pupils too, so calling it hopeless is wrong and dangerous. Brain death requires absent pupillary reflexes, which are present here. A locked-in patient is awake, with preserved vertical eye or eyelid movements, not comatose with absent calorics.

quiz.question: A child with a left temporal abscess becomes drowsy. Over two hours his breathing changes from waxing and waning to fast and deep, the left pupil enlarges and stops reacting, and his flexor posturing becomes extensor. What is happening?
options: Transtentorial herniation, because the level of dysfunction is descending through the brainstem
Recovery, because his breathing is now regular
A new seizure focus in the right hemisphere
A medullary stroke, because breathing has changed
quiz.explanation: Each sign has moved down a level: breathing from the hemispheric pattern to the midbrain pattern, the pupil from reactive to fixed, posture from flexion to extension. A level that descends over hours is herniation until proved otherwise, and a dilating pupil on the side of the abscess fits uncal herniation. This is an emergency. Regular deep breathing here is a sign of midbrain involvement, not recovery. A seizure would not produce a fixed dilated pupil with descending signs. A medullary stroke does not explain a descending sequence that starts in the hemispheres.

quiz.question: Why does a lesion confined to one cerebral hemisphere not usually cause coma on its own?
options: Because the cortex plays no part in consciousness
Because consciousness needs the brainstem activating system and both hemispheres, so one hemisphere's loss leaves the system working
Because hemispheric lesions only affect movement
Because coma always comes from the medulla
quiz.explanation: Wakefulness depends on the interaction between the reticular activating system in the brainstem tegmentum and the cerebral hemispheres. Losing one hemisphere leaves the brainstem system and the other hemisphere working, so the child is impaired but awake. The cortex does take part in consciousness, which is why bilateral hemispheric dysfunction causes coma. Hemispheric lesions affect language, attention, vision and sensation as well as movement. The activating system lies in the pons and midbrain, not the medulla, which is concerned with breathing and circulation.

quiz.question: A resident writes "patient obtunded" in a sedated child's notes. Why does the attending ask for a rewrite?
options: Because obtunded is the wrong grade; the child is stuporous
Because sedated children cannot be assessed
Because labels such as obtunded mean different things to different readers; describing the stimulus and the response lets the next examiner tell whether the child has changed
Because only the coma scale score should be written
quiz.explanation: Brazis recommends describing responsiveness in plain words: the stimulus used, what the child did, and how long it lasted. Labels like obtunded or stuporous are applied inconsistently, so they cannot show a change between examinations, which is the whole point of serial assessment. Swapping one label for another repeats the problem. Sedated children can and must be assessed, with the sedation recorded. A coma scale score is useful but compresses away details, such as which side moves, that matter for localization.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old has two weeks of morning headaches and vomiting. She cannot look up, her eyes rest slightly downward, and she has a mild left sixth-nerve palsy. Which finding best tells you where the lesion is?
options: The failure of upgaze, which points to pressure on the posterior commissure in the pineal region
The left sixth-nerve palsy, which places the lesion in the left pons
Neither, because once the pressure is raised every eye sign is a false localizing sign
The vomiting, which places the lesion in the medulla
quiz.explanation: A tumour pressing on the posterior commissure, such as a pineal tumour, disturbs vertical gaze and can hold the eyes tonically down (Pearl 2014, p. 40), so the upgaze failure is a true address. The sixth-nerve palsy is the tempting answer because it is lateralized, but the sixth nerve is an early casualty of raised pressure from any cause and is the commonest false localizing sign (Pearl 2014, p. 43; Brazis 2011, p. 622). Declaring every eye sign false throws away the one that localizes. Morning vomiting here fits raised pressure rather than a medullary lesion.

signOff: The resident examines a child with depressed consciousness, describes responsiveness in plain words, and states the level of the lesion or that the process is diffuse, with a faculty reader.

opener.parable: When every road is closed, the problem is not on a road. Findings that refuse to agree on a level are not a failure to localize; they are a localization to everywhere.
opener.history: The warning triad of rising intracranial pressure (a slowing pulse, a widening pulse pressure and a change in breathing) carries the name of Harvey Cushing.
